sections.title: What is a BST?
sections.content:
A Binary Search Tree is a binary tree with an ordering property: for every node, all values in the left subtree are strictly smaller, and all values in the right subtree are strictly larger. This invariant holds at every node, not just the root. The property enables binary search on a tree structure - at each node, you compare the target to the node's value and eliminate the entire left or right subtree from consideration. This gives O(log n) search, insert, and delete on a balanced BST.

The most useful property of a BST for interview problems is this: **in-order traversal (left - root - right) gives all values in sorted ascending order**. This single fact makes many problems trivial. Finding the kth smallest element becomes counting nodes in inorder. Checking if two BSTs have the same elements becomes comparing their inorder sequences. Converting a sorted array to a BST means the middle element is the root.

BST operations are O(h) where h is the tree height. On a balanced BST, h = O(log n) and everything is fast. On a degenerate BST - created by inserting elements in sorted order - every node has only one child and h = O(n). The tree becomes a linked list, and search degrades to O(n). This is why self-balancing BSTs (AVL trees, Red-Black trees) exist: they maintain h = O(log n) through rotations during insert and delete.

BST validation is a classic interview problem with a subtle trap. Understanding why the naive local-comparison approach fails, and how the correct min/max range approach works, reveals a deep truth about BST structure: the ordering property is global, not just local between parent and child.

sections.title: When to Use This
sections.content: Use BST techniques when the problem involves a sorted dynamic set: you need to search, insert, and delete while maintaining order. BST inorder traversal applies when you need the kth element, need to process values in sorted order from a tree, or need to validate whether a binary tree has the BST property. BST search applies to problems about finding the closest value, floor (largest value smaller than target), or ceiling (smallest value larger than target) in a BST.
signals: range sum query on sorted data
need to find the count of elements less than / greater than a value, with insertions and deletions interleaved
maintain a running sorted structure over a stream

sections.title: Search/Insert/Delete, Validation, and Inorder Properties
sections.content:
## Search, Insert, Delete - All O(h)

**Search**: compare target to node value. If equal, found. If target < node.val, recurse left. If target > node.val, recurse right. If you reach null, not found.

**Insert**: search for the value. When you reach the null spot where it would have been found, insert there. The new node is always a leaf.

**Delete** has three cases:
- **No children (leaf)**: remove the node by returning null to parent.
- **One child**: bypass the node, returning its single child to the parent.
- **Two children**: find the **in-order successor** (the leftmost node in the right subtree). Copy the successor's value into the current node, then delete the successor from the right subtree.

## Validating a BST - The Min/Max Range

Naive approach (WRONG): check that each node's value is greater than its left child and less than its right child. **This fails** for cases where a node in the right subtree is actually smaller than the root.

Correct approach: pass a `[min, max]` range that each node's value must fall within.
- Root: range is `(-Infinity, +Infinity)`.
- When going left from a node with value v: the range becomes `(min, v)`.
- When going right from a node with value v: the range becomes `(v, max)`.

Use `null` instead of `Integer.MIN_VALUE`/`Integer.MAX_VALUE` to avoid overflow and to handle trees containing those extreme values.

## Inorder Traversal on BSTs

Inorder (left - root - right) on a valid BST produces values in sorted ascending order. Problems that become trivial with this insight:

- **Kth smallest**: run inorder, return the kth element visited.
- **Convert sorted array to BST**: the middle element of each range becomes the root, left half becomes left subtree, right half becomes right subtree. This creates a balanced BST.

## Balanced BSTs - Know They Exist

AVL trees and Red-Black trees maintain h = O(log n) through rotations after insert/delete. You do not need to implement these in interviews. Know: (1) unbalanced BST degenerates to O(n); (2) self-balancing BSTs fix this with O(log n) guaranteed; (3) most standard library sorted sets (Java's `TreeSet`, C++'s `std::set`) are Red-Black trees under the hood.

sections.title: Ordered Set: The Multiset-with-Order-Statistics Pattern
sections.content:
An **ordered set** (also called a sorted multiset, or - in C++ competitive programming - a 'policy tree'/order-statistics tree) is a data structure you reach for constantly once you notice the pattern: you need a dynamic collection that supports insert, delete, AND sorted-order queries (find the k-th smallest, count elements less than x, find the predecessor/successor of x) all in O(log n), simultaneously. A plain hash set gives you O(1) insert/delete but zero ordering information. A plain sorted array gives you O(log n) order queries but O(n) insert/delete (shifting elements). An ordered set is precisely the augmented, self-balancing BST described above (or, in practice, a language's built-in balanced-tree structure - `TreeMap`/`TreeSet` in Java, `SortedList` via a library in Python, `std::multiset` in C++) with subtree-size augmentation at every node, so 'how many elements are less than x' becomes a single root-to-leaf walk summing left-subtree sizes, not a linear scan.

This pattern is enormously common - it's the single largest-by-problem-count gap topic in this roadmap - because so many 'maintain some running statistic over a sliding window or growing stream' problems reduce to exactly this: keep a sorted structure of the current active values, and every query/update touches only the O(log n) neighborhood around one value, never the whole collection. Calendar/booking problems (find if a new interval overlaps existing ones) use an ordered set keyed by interval start to check only the immediate neighbors. 'Closest room/pair' problems use one to binary-search for the nearest value to a query. Sliding-window-median and count-of-smaller-elements problems use one to avoid re-sorting the window on every slide.

sections.title: Core Template
sections.explanation: `countLessOrEqual` is the ordered-set pattern in miniature: because the BST is sorted, the moment `node.val <= x`, the *entire* left subtree also qualifies (all smaller), so it's counted in O(1) via the precomputed `size` field instead of walked - the whole point of the augmentation. In practice you'd reach for a language's built-in balanced structure rather than hand-rolling this, but knowing what it's doing under the hood is what lets you recognize when a problem needs one.

items.name: Self-Balancing BSTs (AVL, Red-Black - Conceptual)
items.description: AVL trees maintain the invariant that the heights of left and right subtrees differ by at most 1, rotating nodes to restore balance after insertions and deletions. Red-Black trees use a coloring scheme with fewer rotations on average. Both guarantee O(log n) height. You will not implement these in interviews but should know they exist and why.

items.name: Convert Sorted Array to BST
items.description: Recursively take the middle element as root, left half as left subtree, right half as right subtree. This produces a height-balanced BST in O(n) time. Directly applies divide-and-conquer thinking to tree construction.
items.example_problem: Convert Sorted Array to Binary Search Tree

items.name: Order Statistics Tree
items.description: An augmented BST where each node stores the size of its subtree. This enables O(log n) kth-smallest queries and O(log n) rank queries. The augmentation is maintained through rotations. Appears in problems requiring dynamic order statistics.
items.example_problem: Kth Smallest Element in a BST

items.name: Ordered Set for Sliding-Window / Streaming Statistics
items.description: Maintain a sorted multiset of the currently active window/stream, so every insert, delete, and 'how many are less than x' query stays O(log n) instead of re-sorting - avoids the O(n) or O(n log n) per-step cost of resorting a plain array on every slide.
items.example_problem: Count of Smaller Numbers After Self

items.name: Ordered Set for Interval / Neighbor Queries
items.description: Keep intervals or points sorted by a key so that checking a new item against its neighbors only (predecessor/successor) is enough to validate overlap or find the closest match - no need to scan every existing item.

sections.title: Complexity
sections.time: O(log n) for search/insert/delete on balanced BST; O(n) worst case on degenerate BST. Ordered-set queries (count less-than, kth-smallest, predecessor/successor) are also O(log n) given subtree-size augmentation.
sections.space: O(h) for recursive call stack during traversal; O(n) to store the tree, plus O(1) extra per node for the augmented size field in an ordered set.
sections.explanation: All BST operations navigate from root to a leaf, taking one step per level. On a balanced BST with h = O(log n), operations are O(log n). When elements are inserted in sorted order, each new node becomes the rightmost leaf, creating a tree of height n - 1. All operations degrade to O(n) - which is exactly why ordered-set problems assume a self-balancing structure (or a language's built-in one) rather than a plain unbalanced BST.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Validating BST with only local parent-child comparison: checking node.val > node.left.val and node.val < node.right.val is wrong. A node deep in the right subtree can be smaller than the root while passing local checks. Always use the min/max range approach.
Using integer MIN/MAX as validation bounds: in JS this is less dangerous, but using extreme sentinel values fails if the tree contains those exact values. Use null to represent 'no constraint'.

Assuming BST is balanced: the problem says 'binary search tree', not 'balanced binary search tree'. Without explicit statement, assume O(n) worst case for height. Do not claim O(log n) unless the tree is stated to be balanced.

Delete with two children - wrong replacement: when deleting a node with two children, you must replace it with the in-order successor (leftmost node in the right subtree). The in-order successor has no left child, making its own deletion a simple case.
In-order gives sorted order ONLY for valid BSTs: if the tree is not a valid BST, in-order traversal does not give sorted order. Confirm the BST property before relying on in-order sorting.

Reaching for a hand-rolled ordered set when the language already provides one - re-implementing a balanced BST from scratch in an interview is rarely the point; know when to reach for a built-in sorted structure instead.
Forgetting to update the subtree-size augmentation on every insert/delete along the path - a stale size field silently breaks every count/kth-smallest query that relies on it.

items.title: Validate Binary Search Tree
items.why: Forces you to confront why local comparison is wrong and implement the min/max range approach. Understanding this is essential before any BST problem.

items.title: Kth Smallest Element in a BST
items.why: Directly applies the inorder-gives-sorted-order property. Solving this in O(h + k) with early termination reinforces how to combine BST structure with inorder traversal.

items.title: Lowest Common Ancestor of a Binary Search Tree
items.why: LCA in a BST uses the BST property directly: if both targets are smaller than the current node, go left. If both larger, go right. Otherwise, current node is the LCA.

items.title: Convert Sorted Array to Binary Search Tree
items.why: Applies divide-and-conquer to BST construction. The middle element is root, recurse on halves - produces a height-balanced BST and reinforces how sorted order maps to BST structure.

items.title: 132 Pattern
items.why: A monotonic-stack solution exists, but an ordered-set-of-seen-minimums approach generalizes better - a good entry point into recognizing the ordered-set pattern outside an explicit BST problem.

items.title: Exam Room
items.why: Maintain seated positions in sorted order so the largest available gap can be found by checking only neighboring seats - a direct ordered-set-for-neighbor-queries problem.

items.title: My Calendar III
items.why: Track the maximum number of overlapping intervals at any point using a sorted structure of interval boundaries - the hardest of the three My Calendar variants.

items.title: Count of Smaller Numbers After Self
items.why: The canonical order-statistics problem - for every element, count how many later elements are smaller, using an order-statistics tree (or BIT/merge-sort as alternatives) for O(n log n) instead of O(n^2).

items.title: Contains Duplicate III
items.why: Needs both a value-range query and an index-window constraint simultaneously - maintain an ordered set of the current window and query its neighbors for anything within the allowed value distance.

sections.title: What to Learn Next
sections.why: Heaps / Priority Queue is the next topic at this level - a natural sibling to BST, reinforcing the same tier of difficulty before moving up.
